findings.title: Working-hours check rejects any slot that falls outside any one range for that day
findings.body: `workingHours.find(cb)` returns true, and the slot is rejected, as soon as the slot lies outside any single working-hour entry whose `days` includes the slot's weekday. A user with split availability on the same days (for example 09:00–12:00 and 13:00–17:00, or a lunch break) has two entries for those days. A slot inside the first range is always outside the second, so `find` matches and `checkIfIsAvailable` returns false. Every slot for such a host is then dropped. The check should pass if the slot lies inside at least one range (`!workingHours.some(contains slot)`), and it should apply only when entries exist for that day. Because `...schedule` is spread into every fixed and loose host check, this regresses ordinary non-round-robin events too.

findings.title: `end` is computed from slotStartTime, so the slot end is never checked against working hours
findings.body: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` is identical to `start`. The intent was clearly the slot end (`slotEndTime`). As written, `end > workingHour.endTime` is just a check on the start time, so a slot that starts inside working hours but runs past their end passes. The check is effectively broken.

findings.title: Multiple date-override ranges on the same day make every slot unavailable
findings.body: The `dateOverrides.find` callback returns true (slot unavailable) as soon as the slot is outside any single override on that date. A host with two override ranges on one day (for example 09:00–12:00 and 14:00–17:00) has each valid slot fail the other range's checks. A 10:00 slot is before the 14:00 range and so returns true, and the function returns false. The slot has to be rejected only if it fits none of the overrides for that date. Cal.com's date-override UI allows multiple ranges per date, so this makes valid slots disappear for those hosts.

findings.title: Object identity comparison with `===` on dayjs objects is always false
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)` compares two freshly created objects by reference, so it never evaluates to true. This branch was meant to handle a zero-length override (the day marked unavailable). It is dead code, so that case relies on the later `isBefore`/`isAfter` checks. Compare with `.isSame()` or `.valueOf()`.

findings.title: Override matched by UTC calendar date of its start only; overrides crossing UTC midnight are skipped
findings.body: After shifting the override start to real UTC, the code matches an override to a slot only if the UTC date of the override start equals the UTC date of the slot start. An override that spans UTC midnight is common for hosts far from UTC, for example 06:00–12:00 in Sydney, which runs from 20:00Z the previous day to 02:00Z. Slots on the later UTC date never match, so `dateOverrideExist` stays false. Those slots fall through to the regular working-hours check and the override is ignored for them. The comparison should use the organizer-local date, or check whether the slot falls inside the [start, end) instant range.

findings.title: Override-to-day filter is not timezone-adjusted, but the time conversion now is
findings.body: `activeOverrides` still selects overrides whose raw `start` (the organizer's wall-clock time encoded as UTC) falls between the invitee's start and end of day. The new code then shifts the minutes by the invitee-vs-organizer offset. The day selection and the time conversion therefore use different frames. For an invitee far ahead of the organizer (for example UTC+10 and an organizer in IST), the override's real instant is on invitee day D, but the raw start falls on D+1. The override is dropped from day D and applied to D+1 at the shifted time. The filter should run on the converted start, using the same offset.

findings.title: Shifted override minutes wrap at midnight, producing inverted or wrongly-placed ranges
findings.body: Start and end are converted to `hour()*60 + minute()` after adding the offset, which discards the day. If the shift pushes an override across the invitee's midnight, start and end wrap to small values. A late-evening override such as 18:00–23:59 in the organizer's timezone, viewed from a timezone further east, can give an end value smaller than the start, which `buildSlots` skips (`start >= end`), so the slots vanish. If only one side wraps, the range is placed on the wrong day. Clamp or split the range at the invitee's day boundaries instead of taking time-of-day modulo 24h.

findings.title: Offset derived from `Date.toString()` and possibly undefined timeZone
findings.body: `dayjs(override.start.toString())` re-parses a host-locale string such as 'Tue Jul 04 2023 14:00:00 GMT+0000 (...)'. That is implementation-dependent and drops milliseconds; pass `override.start` directly. `override.timeZone` is optional in the updated `TimeRange` type. When it is missing, `.tz(undefined)` silently falls back to the runtime's local timezone, giving a different offset on client and server.

findings.title: No test for the headline fix (fixed-host date overrides in round-robin)
findings.body: The PR's main fix is that fixed hosts' date overrides and working hours are enforced in `checkIfIsAvailable` for round-robin events. The only new test is a personal-event invitee-timezone case. Nothing covers a ROUND_ROBIN event with a fixed host having an override, multiple overrides on one day, split working hours, or an override spanning UTC midnight. Those are the cases where the bugs above show up. Also, `toHaveTimeSlots` only iterates the actual slots, so a result with fewer slots than expected still passes.
